background.definition: Dengue fever is a self-limited, febrile illness, but dengue hemorrhagic fever involves prominent hemorrhagic manifestations associated with thrombocytopenia and an increased vascular permeability.

list.listitem: WHO estimates 390 million Dengue virus infections per year.
The number of cases reported to WHO in 2019 was 4.2 million.
There are 250,000 to 500,000 cases of DHF reported to World Health Organization annually.
A systematic review found that the prevalence of dengue virus in blood supplies was as high as 2.8% in some series.
DF and DHF are caused by 1 of 5 virus serotypes (DEN-1, DEN-2, DEN-3, DEN-4, DEN-5) of the genus Flavivirus.
Secondary infections are more likely to constitute a risk factor for DHF.

The disease is endemic to tropical and subtropical zones, including Mexico, portions of the southwestern United States, the Caribbean, Central America, much of South America, south and southeast Asia, Africa, and northeast Australia.
Temperature changes and rainfall are important climate factors for viral reproduction and host adult mosquito breeding and activity.
The primary vector of DF is the Aedes mosquito, most commonly Aedes aegypti.

Major hallmarks distinguishing DHF from DF and other viral hemorrhagic fevers are plasma leakage from increased vascular permeability and abnormal hemostasis. Hypovolemic shock can occur from critical plasma volume loss.
Consumptive coagulopathy, leading to DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) in its most extreme form, can also occur.
Thrombocytopenia is caused by dengue virus-induced bone marrow suppression and an immune-mediated platelet destruction.
Prevention of mosquito bites is crucial. A
It is important to emphasize that spraying does not obviate the need for environmental mosquito control measures or personal precautions.

A cluster randomized trial in Indonesia randomized 24 geographic regions to either deployment of wMel-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitos (less susceptible to dengue virus infection) or no deployment. Anyone living in the regions with symptomatic undifferentiated fever were tested for dengue virus infection. The intervention successfully reduced the percentage of febrile patients with dengue (67/2905 vs 318/3401, 2.3% vs 9.4%, p = 0.004, NNT = 14). Hospitalization was also less likely (0.4% vs 3.0%, p < 0.05, NNT = 38). B

A tetravalent dengue vaccine is effective, and has been evaluated in children as well. In a study in Central and South America, the vaccine was 65% effective (1.0 vs 2.9 cases of dengue/100 person-years). Trials in Asia and Latin America had similar results.
A

A tetravalent vaccine candidate (TAK-003) was evaluated in 20,071 persons randomized in a 2:1 ratio to 2 doses of vaccine or placebo 3 months apart. In the per protocol analysis of all participants getting at least one dose (95% of the entire study population), the vaccine was 80% effective against symptomatic infection and 95% effective against hospitalization. The vaccine was well tolerated.
DF is self-limited and is characterized by acute febrile illness of 2 to 7 days associated with headache, myalgias, rash, and capillary fragility. C
DHF is distinguished by hemorrhagic manifestations and increased vascular permeability. C

A study comparing the 1997 and 2009 WHO dengue case definitions found that the newer case definition is easier to use and better able to classify severe cases of dengue.
Dengue without warning signs: Fever and two of the following: nausea or vomiting, rash, aches and pains, leukopenia, or positive tourniquet test. Dengue with warning signs: Dengue as defined above with any of the following: abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion), mucosal bleeding, lethargy or restlessness, liver enlargement >2 cm, or increase in hematocrit concurrent with rapid decrease in platelet count. Severe dengue: Dengue with at least one of the following criteria: severe plasma leakage leading to shock and fluid accumulation with respiratory distress OR severe bleeding as evaluated by the clinician OR severe organ involvement (AST or ALT ≥1000, impaired consciousness, or failure of heart and other organs).
Incubation period is typically 3-14 days, 7 days on average.

Typical symptoms of DF include fever, constitutional signs, rash, and gastrointestinal symptoms. A study of 3926 patients with laboratory-diagnosed dengue in Puerto Rico showed the following symptoms: fever, joint pain, headache, eye pain, body pain, rash, gastrointestinal symptoms , and respiratory symptoms.
Physical examination is generally nonspecific. Fever and rash are often present. Hepatomegaly, pharyngeal erythema, conjunctival injection, and lymphadenopathy are observed in 20% to 50% of patients.

Patients with hemorrhagic DF commonly show signs of increased vascular permeability, such as hemoconcentration, pleural effusion, or ascites. Severe thrombocytopenia and elevation of aminotransferases commonly results. Plasma leakage may also occur with nonspecific findings, most commonly abdominal pain.

Spontaneous petechiae or ecchymoses were found in approximately half of adults and children with DHF in Cuba. Other findings include: hematemesis (15%-30% of patients), metrorrhagia (40% of women), melena (5%-10%), and epistaxis (10%).

Consider the tourniquet test to assess for DHF. Inflate the blood pressure cuff midway between systolic and diastolic blood pressure for 5 minutes. A positive test is more than 20 petechiae/square inch and suggests DHF.
If DF is suspected, consider a CBC, a platelet count, and serum aspartate transaminase (AST). Patients with DHF may have hemoconcentration.

Leukopenia is common. Thrombocytopenia is common, with platelet counts <100,000 in 16% to 55% of patients. One study suggests if no signs of leukopenia or thrombocytopenia, that influenza is more likely than DF.
AST is commonly elevated. Marked elevations have been recorded (5-15 times normal), and in one study in Thailand 96% of patients with suspected DHF but a normal AST did not have the disease.

Laboratory criteria for confirmation of DF are: isolation of dengue virus from serum or autopsy; demonstration of 4-fold or greater change in reciprocal IgG or IgM antibody titers to one or more dengue virus antigens in paired serum samples; demonstration of dengue virus antigen in autopsy tissue, serum, or cerebrospinal fluid samples by immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, or ELISA; or detection of dengue virus genomic sequences in autopsy tissue serum or cerebrospinal fluid samples by PCR.

Immunoassays of virus-specific IgG antibodies have shown a sensitivity and specificity of 99% and 96%. MAC-ELISA IgM test has much lower sensitivity and specificity. In one study of Thai children, only 29% of patients had a positive result on the ELISA test.In another study, sensitivities ranged from 31% to 54% for the ELISPOT-MNT and SD Bioline Dengue Deuo tests.
If DHF is suspected, additional signs of increased vascular permeability may manifest as pleural effusion or ascites in radiographs.

To diagnose DF, look for acute febrile illness of 2 to 7 days with 2 of more of the following: headache, retroorbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia, rash, leukopenia, capillary fragility on tourniquet test, or mild hemorrhagic manifestations.

To diagnose DHF, look for probable dengue plus one or more of the following: high-positive tourniquet test; petechiae, ecchymosis, or purpura; bleeding from mucosae or other sites; thrombocytopenia; evidence of plasma leakage.
To diagnose dengue shock syndrome, look for all of the DHF criteria plus signs of circulatory failure.
Provide supportive care. C
No drug therapy has been shown to help. B
A systematic review found insufficient evidence regarding corticosteroids for the treatment of shock in DHF. A
A clinical trial of celgosivir in 50 adults found no benefit clinically or in terms of viral load.

A systematic review identified 8 RCTs of the use of corticosteroids for dengue infection. In 4 studies of children with dengue related shock, there was no benefit with regards to death, need for transfusion, pulmonary hemorrhage, seizures, or length of hospital stay. In 4 studies of adults and children with early stage dengue (no shock or sepsis), there was no evidence of benefit with regards to mortality, complications, progression, bleeding, thrombocytopenia, ascities, or need for intensive care.
NSAIDs should be avoided as they may increase the risk of hemorrhagic complications.
DF is usually mild in children. In some adults it can be incapacitating with severe bone pain ("break-bone fever") and prolonged fever. B
The mortality rate is 1% to 5% for DHF. B
Avoid aspirin in children because of the risk of Reye's syndrome.
